messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: programming user-defined functions (C++, or another language)
parts:
Hi,

1. I need to implement a function that is very complex, and uses a
numerical, iterative algorithm. My understanding is that I need to
program a C++ function for this, that implements the function and its
Jacobian, compile and link it to Stan. However, this is just a broad
outline, and I am wondering if there is a tutorial or an example.

2. Technically, if the function is f:R^N -> R^M, and I can calculate
f(x) and the Jacobian at x, for x which is a vector of doubles, is that
enough?

3. Ideally, I would like to implement the function not in C++, but
Julia, which has a C interface, which I believe that I can somehow patch
into a C++ interface that Stan can call. Is there an a priori problem
with this? I know this is more hassle and I will need to get my hands
dirty, but I am more comfortable with Julia than C++. I will make the
code available but it is for a paper, so I don't aim to integrate it
into Stan (I am just mentioning this to make it clear that the toolchain
nightmare will be mine, not anyone else's).

Best,

Tamas

Embedding interpreters in C++ is something that people do. Here's a blog
post about doing it with Python
http://www.codeproject.com/Articles/11805/Embedding-Python-in-C-C-Part-I,
and I noticed this thread on the Julia list "Embed julia in C/C++"
http://julia-programming-language.2336112.n4.nabble.com/Embed-julia-in-C-C-td3339.html

Others can weigh in but I suspect your best bet would be to fork the
Stan codebase and add your function (writing it in C++ strikes me as
easier than dealing with the embedding problem).

Best,

Allen

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] programming user-defined functions (C++, or another language)
parts:
Just wanted to respond to #1:

On Sep 23, 2015 11:54 AM, "Tamas Papp" <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> 1. I need to implement a function that is very complex, and uses a
> numerical, iterative algorithm. My understanding is that I need to
> program a C++ function for this, that implements the function and its
> Jacobian, compile and link it to Stan. However, this is just a broad
> outline, and I am wondering if there is a tutorial or an example.

You can write the function in Stan. If there's an iterative algorithm, that doesn't necessarily pose a problem. The autodiff will work through the iterative algorithm. (One of the benefits of autodiff compared to symbolic differentiation.)

There might be some speed gains if you implemented it in c++ directly, especially if you have the gradients with respect to all the parameters of the model, but if it were me, I'd start with a full Stan implementation.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] programming user-defined functions (C++, or another language)
parts:
This is exactly what Michael was warning against --- naively
autodiffing an iterative algorithm. And both Michael and Daniel
are right. It can work to just autodiff an iterative algorithm,
but it can have bad numerical properties. So it's better in terms of
both efficiency and numerical stability to write a separate iterative
algorithm for the derivative that takes its numerical properties
into account.

I also want to qualify that for a full Stan implementation of
a function, you need not only first-order derivatives, but also
second- and third-order. Those usually come about through a templated
implementation of fvar<T> where T is either a var or fvar<var>.
But the same logic applies there --- autodiffing the first-order
Jacobian code to get the Hessian may not be stable. But if all you
need to do is HMC, you can get by with just the var implementation,
which only needs the Jacobian.

Yes, the Stan Math Library is full of examples in C++.

I'm guessing the Julia to Stan combo shot will require you to know
more about C++, not less, than implementing it in C++ directly.

- Bob

Right --- the Jacobian's just because it may be a function
mapping N inputs to M outputs, so we need M gradients. Often
it's more efficient to do them all at once, as in many of the
matrix implemntations now (many of which used to just autodiff
the algorithms).

- Bob
